particularites.text: Offset fiscal year: Broadcom closes its fiscal year in early November (the Sunday closest to 31 October), not in December. The years in the table therefore denote fiscal years (e.g. 'FY2025' = year ended 2 November 2025), not calendar years - handled by the fyEndMonth=11 field.

Extreme customer concentration in the AI segment: a handful of mega-customers (Google, Meta, and now Anthropic, OpenAI through multi-year custom silicon agreements) accounts for the bulk of the growth in AI semiconductor revenue. This dependence is a source of major asymmetry (upside if the orders materialise, downside if a hyperscaler internalises or defers its investment) - an idiosyncratic risk factor carried in hypothese.text rather than quantified in the adjXXX.

points.sujet: Gross margin resilience in the face of the low-margin TPU/rack mix
points.ancienPropos: Q1 FY26 (04/03/2026, direct answer to a question on the risk of margin compression tied to low-margin racks (45-50% gross margin), Timothy Arcuri UBS): Hock Tan categorically dismisses the risk, stating that 'the AI products will not be affected by gross margin'; CFO Kirsten Spears adds that the mix impact 'will not be substantial'.
points.nouveauPropos: Q2 FY26 (03/06/2026, answer to a question on gross margin drivers, Ross Seymore Deutsche Bank): the CFO explicitly confirms that TPU/ASIC products carry LOWER margins than networking (described as 'very margin-rich'), and although the CEO describes the semiconductor segment's margins as 'structurally very stable and solid', he now attributes an observed consolidated compression to the 'mix shift from software to semiconductors' - a nuance absent from the March narrative, which categorically dismissed any mix impact on the margin.
points.justification: The margin is a central pillar of the thesis (marginLeverage anchor); the move from a categorical denial ('not affected', 'not substantial') to an explicit acknowledgement that TPU/ASIC is structurally less margin-rich than networking and that a mix shift is already compressing consolidated margins, without management revisiting its March remarks, deserves to be tracked - the current modelling (marginLeverage anchor, medium confidence, gradual rather than immediate margin expansion) remains compatible with both narratives, but the CFO now qualifies a risk he dismissed entirely three months earlier.

clesRetenues: Q Blayne Curtis (Jefferies) - does the '>100 Md$' AI target for 2027 exclude networking and racks, investor pessimism on hyperscaler ROI given the growth trajectory: Hock Tan specifies that the figure covers silicon chips (XPU, switches, DSP), stresses that the customers are not only hyperscalers but also LLM developers building platforms, demand strong and driven by training AND inference.

Q Harlan Sur (JPMorgan) - do customers' in-house chip initiatives (COT) threaten Broadcom's position, how to maintain a 12-18 month technology lead: Hock stresses silicon design complexity, advanced packaging and manufacturing scale as barriers, no competitor can match the 'track record' of delivering XPUs in high volumes with very high yields.

Q Ross Seymore (Deutsche Bank) - drivers of the AI networking share at 40% of AI revenue, is networking included in the '>100 Md$', how networking leadership reinforces the XPU positioning: Hock cites demand for Tomahawk 6 switches and the 200G SerDes, projects an AI networking share of 33 to 40% of total AI revenue, customers targeting 200G then 400G.

Q Christopher Muse (Cantor Fitzgerald) - workload disaggregation (prefill/decode separation) and a potential shift from GPU to custom silicon: Hock explains that XPUs are increasingly tailored to specific workloads (e.g. mixture-of-experts), unlike GPUs on dense matrix multiplication, which improves efficiency.

Q Timothy Arcuri (UBS) - concern that a mix of low-margin racks (45-50% gross margin) would drive the consolidated margin down by 500 basis points, what is the gross margin floor: Hock dismisses the premise, states that yields and costs have been optimised and that 'the AI products will not be affected by gross margin'; Kirsten Spears adds that the mix impact 'will not be substantial'.

Q Stacy Rasgon (Bernstein) - attempt to reconstruct the calculation of the '>100 Md$' 2027 target via gigawatt deployments and the $/GW content (~20 Md$/GW), is the method correct: Hock confirms the approach, acknowledges high variability in $/GW across customers, indicates around 10 GW of deployment expected in 2027.

Q Benjamin Reitzes (Melius Research) - how Broadcom secured component capacity through to 2028 (substrates, HBM, wafers) ahead of its competitors, is the visibility sufficient for 2028 growth: Hock stresses the early booking of advanced substrates and partnerships; Charlie Kawwas adds that the multi-year commitments with the six custom silicon customers provide 2 to 4 years of visibility on their roadmaps.

Q Vivek Arya (BofA) - split of the Anthropic 20 Md$/GW deal between chips and racks, how Broadcom maintains its market share visibility in a fragmented multi-vendor environment: Hock distinguishes strategic custom XPU programmes from the transactional cloud GPU business, stresses that these six customers regard XPU development as 'strategic, not optional', with very clear visibility on their roadmaps.

Q Tom O'Malley (Barclays) - why Broadcom is promoting direct attach copper (DAC) via 400G SerDes despite its leadership in co-packaged optics (CPO), adoption of the scale-up Ethernet protocol: Hock explains that DAC offers the lowest latency, power and cost for scale-up clusters; Charlie Kawwas confirms that Ethernet is the de facto standard for scale-out and an emerging choice for XPU scale-up.

Q Jim Schneider (Goldman Sachs) - do the custom XPU commitments outside TPU mainly target inference, performance/cost advantages vs GPU justifying the large-scale forecasts: Hock notes that customers often start with inference (lower compute needs and cost), but indicates that the majority is now developing separate chips for training and inference simultaneously.

Q Joshua Buchalter (TD Cowen) - how visibility has improved over 1-2 quarters to allow more detailed customer forecasts, does the OpenAI announcement of '>1 GW in 2027' imply a sharp inflection in 2028 given the 10 GW/2029 deal: Hock attributes the improved visibility to growing customer confidence as XPUs prove their capabilities and align with strategic roadmaps, reaffirms that XPU is a 'durable strategic bet' rather than transactional.

Q Harlan Sur (JPMorgan) - reconciliation of the FY26 AI revenue guidance of 56 Md$ with an H2 announced at 2x H1, does the 18-month order book now exceed 200 Md$: management specifies H1 AI revenue of around 19 Md$, an H2 at 2x giving ~38 Md$ (total ~56 Md$); for 2027 the CEO reiterates the '>100 Md$' target without quarterly detail, noting momentum intact if not stronger.

Q Blayne Curtis (Jefferies) - scope of the long-term agreement with Google (fixed volume or possible upside), confidence on market share at that customer: Hock stresses a 'very substantial dollar amount', acknowledges that Google will probably source from several suppliers given the growth in AI consumption, but Broadcom's commitment remains 'very substantial'.

Q Ross Seymore (Deutsche Bank) - gross margin drivers within semiconductors (XPU vs networking), does the margin pressure continue into 2027: the CFO explains that TPU/ASIC products carry lower margins than networking (described as 'very margin-rich'); the CEO insists on semiconductor margins being 'structurally very stable and solid', the consolidated compression being attributed to the mix shift from software to semiconductors.

Q Benjamin Reitzes (Melius) - evolution of the TAM per gigawatt as compute content increases, does that accelerate beyond current guidance: the CEO indicates a 'relatively stable' $/GW (more powerful chips reducing unit volumes) but gigawatt demand itself accelerating sharply, with 2027-2028 trajectories suggesting growth beyond current forecasts.

Q Timothy Arcuri (UBS) - security of wafer and HBM supply if customers ask for incremental volume, alternative foundry options considered: the CEO says he is comfortable on securing supply through to 2028-2029 and confirms the ability to meet incremental capacity requests, without detailing an alternative foundry strategy.

Q Stacy Rasgon (Bernstein) - gigawatt delivery targets for 2027 vs the previous guidance, is the split weighted towards the second half: the CEO confirms a 2027 planning target of around 10 GW, unchanged vs the previous quarter, with an H2 weighting, opening an 'interesting' trajectory towards 2028 with markedly higher volumes.

Q Jim Schneider (Goldman Sachs) - profile of the networking share of AI revenue over 2026-2027, timing of optical/CPO revenue materialising: the CEO indicates that the current networking share of 40% represents an 'abnormal' peak, expects a normalisation 'more around 30%' as the XPU ramp accelerates.

Q Tom O'Malley (Barclays) - is Broadcom playing a chip 'backstop' role in future customer deals, future AI infrastructure financing models: the CEO corrects the characterisation, specifying that Broadcom supplies TPU chips and compute directly to customers such as Anthropic rather than playing a third-party guarantee role.

Q CJ Muse (Cantor Fitzgerald) - interest in niche derivative XPU markets (interconnect, storage) vs large-scale core platforms: the CEO reaffirms a focused model: supplying XPU accelerators and critical clustering components (switches, PCIe, DSP, lasers) exclusively to LLM developers, with the financing vehicles supporting frontier model labs rather than scattered enterprise buyers.

Q AT Malik (Citi) - impact of AI/generative AI on infrastructure software growth, renewals and long-term trajectory: the CEO reports no negative impact, on the contrary VMware growth accelerated by the deployment of CPU/GPU volumes, expects sustained VMware momentum for several quarters, structural insulation tied to the positioning of the hypervisor layer.

Q Edward Snyder (Charter Equity Research) - do enterprise AI adoption and access to models via the cloud (Bedrock, Vertex) represent a second wave of demand distinct from the hyperscalers' internal workloads: the CEO acknowledges an emerging enterprise AI consumption but stresses that the tokens purchased flow through the API platforms of the same frontier labs (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google), the bulk of demand ultimately coming from those centralised developers rather than from a scattered enterprise deployment.

Q Joe Moore (Morgan Stanley) - explanation of the 30 Md$ of bookings vs the near-term shipment pace, drivers of the visibility extended through to 2028: the CEO attributes the bookings to forward planning covering compute, memory, HBM, power and infrastructure, stresses customers 'placing orders early' in 'strong demand', extending visibility to '2028 now' against 2027 previously.

Q Joshua Buchalter (TD Cowen) - evolution of revenue per gigawatt given the earlier guidance of 15-20 Md$, how price and content evolve from generation to generation: the CEO projects sharply higher content per gigawatt driven by rising XPU prices, the integration of CPU cores, multi-die architectures and HBM integration, with these changes showing up from generation to generation rather than quarter by quarter.

dernierCall.guidanceProchainTrimestre: Q3 FY26: consolidated revenue ~$29.4B (+84% y/y) - semiconductors ~$20.5B (+124%), of which AI $16.0B (+200%+ y/y); infrastructure software ~$8.9B (+31%). Consolidated gross margin down to ~74% (pure mix effect, 'not a structural change'), operating margin stable ~67%, adjusted EBITDA ~68%, non-GAAP tax rate ~16%.
dernierCall.guidanceAnnuelle: No formal total-revenue FY guidance, but FY26 AI semiconductor revenue target ~$56B (+~180% vs FY25; H2 = 2x the ~$19B shipped in H1) and FY27 AI revenue reiterated 'in excess of $100B', with further AI growth expected in FY28 (~10GW of shipments planned in 2027, back-half loaded; 'a lot more gigawatts' in 2028).
pointsCles: AI semiconductor revenue hit a record $10.8B (+143% y/y, above outlook; networking ~40% of AI revenue) within record total revenue of $22.2B (+48%); AI bookings exceeded $30B in the quarter and management's visibility now extends to 2028 (vs 2027 three months ago).

Program status across the 6 core customers: long-term multi-generation TPU agreement with Google ('very substantial dollars'); >1GW of Broadcom TPU compute for Anthropic in 2026 plus 5GW of next-gen TPU from 2027; OpenAI silicon delivered with production late 2026 and 1.3GW contractually committed for 2027 (within the 10GW-by-2029 deal); Meta MTIA partnership of 3GW through 2028 with the first 1GW order received; $6B of purchase orders from the two other customers.

Launch of the 'AI XPV' platform with Apollo, Blackstone and other investors to finance >20GW of compute capacity through 2028 for frontier labs (first tranche $35B via Apollo); business model emphatically reaffirmed as 'chips only' - no racks or integrated systems - which, together with the unraised $100B+ FY27 AI target, drove the ~-15% post-print stock reaction despite record results.

Record operating margin 67.3% and record FCF $10.3B (46% of revenue); Q3 gross margin guided down to ~74% on pure semiconductor/software mix (management urges modeling the two segments' margins separately); CFO Kirsten Spears retired June 12, succeeded by Amie Thuener (ex-Google).

hypothese.summary: A bet on the continued explosion in custom AI semiconductor revenue (accelerators + networking) at a handful of hyperscalers, underpinned by the highly profitable and recurring base of infrastructure software (VMware); a high valuation that leaves little margin for error on execution of the AI pipeline.
hypothese.text:
== THESIS SUMMARY ==
With Nvidia, one of the two pillars of AI compute infrastructure - via a different model: custom accelerators (ASIC) plus the networking around them, for a handful of hyperscalers seeking Nvidia independence. The central bet is the materialization of a colossal AI pipeline (>30bn AI bookings in Q2 FY26 alone; >100bn AI semi revenue targeted for FY27) on named multi-year deals (Google, Meta, Anthropic, OpenAI), backed by the far more stable VMware-anchored infrastructure-software pillar.

== THESIS READ ==
- The FY27 >100bn AI target is the thesis fulcrum - Q3 (early Sept) and Q4 prints must show the ramp steepening. Watch: AI revenue per quarter vs the implied ramp.
- Customer concentration is extreme by design (a handful of hyperscalers) - one program slip moves a year. Watch: any named-deal calendar change.
- Deleveraging proceeds (net debt 49.6bn -> net cash by 2030 modeled) while dilution continues (+0.8%/yr, SBC). Watch: buyback resumption vs further M&A appetite.

== SPECIAL FACTORS ==
Fiscal year ends late October. Base = NORMALIZED GAAP: acquisition-intangible amortization (~7.9bn/yr) and SBC (~8.5bn/yr) are REINTEGRATED per E5 (serial acquirer - these charges are structurally recurring), unlike the management non-GAAP. Omnium EPS is therefore structurally ~40% below the non-GAAP consensus - a definitional wedge, documented in the scorecard, not a divergence call. FY24 tax one-off retreated from 'data'; FY25 carries a ~+1.6bn tax one-off (ETR ~5-6% on IP onshoring), documented in the bridge.

== PARAMETERS & WATCH-LIST ==
FY26: revenue 74.4bn, EBIT 34.4bn (GAAP base); FY27-FY30: AI ramp decelerating per aiRampDecel ancrage, margin leverage per marginLeverage; ETR 24% normative; finNet declining with deleveraging. Watch: Q3 FY26 (Sept) - first post-refresh anchor; AI bookings conversion; VMware renewal economics; tax-rate normalization pace.

== CATALYSTS ==
Q3 FY26 (early Sept); FY27 AI revenue framing at the Q4 report (Dec); new named ASIC customers; networking share gains (Tomahawk/Jericho).

ancrages.moteur: Ramp-up of AI semiconductor revenue (custom accelerators + networking) driven by a named multi-year pipeline (Google, Meta, Anthropic, OpenAI): very strong total revenue growth in the near term (Q3 FY26 guidance +84% y/y) then a gradual deceleration as the base grows, from about +55% in FY26 towards ~+18% in FY30; the VMware software base (~+8-9%/yr, recurring) cushions semi cyclicality.

Strong operating leverage: GAAP operating margin expanding continuously with the rise of the AI and high-margin software mix (non-GAAP guidance ~67%; on a GAAP basis, projected operating margin rising from ~46% in FY26 towards ~52% in FY30 as PPA amortisation stabilises as a % of growing revenue).

EBIT->Net bridge on a normalised tax basis: normalised GAAP effective rate of ~13-15% retained (excluding the FY24 one-off tax item of ~4,5 Md$ adjusted out upstream), net interest expense ~3,0 Md$/yr edging down with post-VMware deleveraging; projected Net/EBIT conversion ratio ~78-82%.

Diluted share count structurally edging higher (high SBC ~8,5 Md$/yr exceeding buybacks), historically ~+1%/yr post 10-for-1 split (July 2024); projected at ~+0,8%/yr, tempered by a moderate buyback programme.

2025.residualNote: FY25 effective GAAP tax ran ~5-6% (IP-onshoring deferred-tax effects) vs the 12% used here - the +1.6bn residual is a documented tax one-off, consistent with the FY24 tax one-off already retreated from 'data'. Projections use 24% normative GAAP.

The wedge is definitional, tracked, and must not be read as a miss.
